title: Silver crossing west, silk crossing east: the Acapulco-Manila galleon, 1565-1815
register: documentary, and wary of the treasure-ship legend
summary: One Crown-chartered ship a year tied Manila to Acapulco for two hundred fifty years: American silver went west to buy Chinese silk, Indian cotton, and Japanese lacquer, and Asian merchandise came east on the returning tornaviaje alongside friars, officials, and a colonial subsidy. The system held together Chinese merchant credit, Mexican capital, coerced Philippine labor, and a single fragile sailing window each year, and it did not end from decline but from the collapse of the Mexican fiscal and political order that made an annual Acapulco crossing possible.

nodes.name: Manila
nodes.note: The colonial capital after 1571, and the commercial exchange where Chinese junks unloaded, Manila merchants bought and bargained, and the annual cargo allocation to the galleon was assessed. Its population and food supply depended on Chinese residents confined to successive Pariáns outside the walled city.

nodes.name: Cavite
nodes.note: The naval base and final loading point on Manila Bay, where hulls were built and caulked and cargo was transferred by lighter for galleons too deep-drafted to work the shallow Pasig waterfront. Timber, cordage, and provisions converged here from across Luzon and the Visayas.

nodes.name: Acapulco
nodes.note: The American terminus, a small port that swelled for weeks each year into a fair town when the galleon arrived, its customs officers checking registers against holds while muleteers and Mexico City agents converged on the coast. The last secure traditional arrival is placed in 1811, disrupted by the Mexican insurgency before the Crown's 1813 decree formally ended the monopoly.

nodes.name: Mexico City
nodes.note: The financial center of the American side of the trade. Its wholesale merchant houses advanced silver, kept Manila correspondents, and often controlled cargo nominally reserved for Manila residents, so the formal monopoly and the capital actually behind it were never quite the same thing.

nodes.name: Veracruz
nodes.note: The Atlantic gateway where selected Asian goods, having crossed New Spain overland, joined the Spanish treasure fleets bound for Seville and later Cádiz. The galleon itself never called here; this was always a change of carrier.

nodes.name: Seville
nodes.note: Seat of the Casa de la Contratación and the destination of Asian goods that completed the crossing of New Spain, until the early eighteenth-century administrative shift moved the American trade's formal center to Cádiz.

nodes.name: Cádiz
nodes.note: Successor to Seville as the Atlantic terminus after the early eighteenth-century reorganization, and later the home port from which the Royal Philippine Company sailed its rival ships around the Cape rather than through Mexico.

nodes.name: Yuegang (Haicheng), Fujian
nodes.note: The chief embarkation region for the junks that supplied Manila with silk, porcelain, and manufactured goods, its exact ports shifting with Ming and Qing maritime restrictions until Xiamen's later rise. Southern Fujianese merchants bore the piracy, typhoon, and regulatory risk of the crossing, and extended credit to Manila buyers through kinship and godparent ties.

nodes.name: Xiamen
nodes.note: Rose to prominence as a Manila-facing port after the Ming-Qing transition and the loosening of maritime restrictions, gradually displacing the older Yuegang-Haicheng complex as the chief Fujianese departure point.

nodes.name: Macao
nodes.note: A Portuguese entrepôt that fed Manila with Chinese and wider Asian merchandise, especially when direct Chinese shipping was constrained, and that connected the Spanish trade to Goa, Malacca, and Japan despite Spanish law's nominal exclusion of foreign carriers.

nodes.name: Nagasaki
nodes.note: Supplied Manila with silver, copper, lacquer, and textiles in the late sixteenth and early seventeenth centuries, and carried missionaries, Japanese Christian exiles, and mercenaries alongside the merchandise. Tokugawa maritime restrictions and the suppression of Christianity narrowed the direct connection after the 1630s, though indirect Japanese goods kept circulating.

nodes.name: Ternate, Moluccas
nodes.note: Source of the cloves and other spices that reached Manila directly or through Chinese and Portuguese intermediaries, one node in the wider Southeast Asian and Indian Ocean supply feeding the eastbound cargo.

nodes.name: Batavia, Java
nodes.note: Representative of the Javanese and Malay trade in pepper, textiles, aromatics, and provisions that reached Manila through Chinese and other intermediaries rather than by a direct Spanish line.

nodes.name: Ayutthaya, Siam
nodes.note: Siamese and Cambodian forest products, ceramics, food, and textiles reached Manila through this trade, generally by way of Chinese shipping rather than direct Spanish contact.

nodes.name: Madras
nodes.note: Stands for the Coromandel cotton-textile trade that reached Manila indirectly, through Chinese and Portuguese intermediaries; cargo labeled 'China goods' often obscures this Indian and wider Asian origin.

nodes.name: Hooghly, Bengal
nodes.note: Bengal supplied cotton textiles and enslaved people who reached Manila and, from there, New Spain, through intermediary Portuguese and Asian shipping rather than a direct Spanish route.

nodes.name: Surat, Gujarat
nodes.note: A Gujarati source of cotton textiles reaching Manila through Portuguese and other intermediaries, part of the wider Indian Ocean supply feeding the galleon's eastbound cargo.

nodes.name: Colombo, Ceylon
nodes.note: Source of gems, cinnamon, and ivory reaching Manila through intermediary shipping; enslaved Ceylonese people also appear among the network's coerced eastbound passengers.

nodes.name: Puebla
nodes.note: A manufacturing and redistribution center on the road between Acapulco and Veracruz, where Asian goods were consumed, reworked into local craft, and forwarded onward through New Spain.

nodes.name: San Blas
nodes.note: A Pacific naval and communications port developed in the later eighteenth century that supplemented, and during war and the Mexican insurgency sometimes substituted for, Acapulco.

nodes.name: Callao and Lima
nodes.note: The major market for Chinese silks that the Crown repeatedly tried and failed to close off, fearing silver drainage and injury to Seville's merchants. Asian goods reached it from New Spain through contraband, licenses, and false declarations despite standing prohibitions.

nodes.name: Havana
nodes.note: The convoy junction where goods and correspondence that had crossed New Spain from Acapulco joined the Atlantic fleets bound for Seville and later Cádiz.

nodes.name: Guam, Marianas
nodes.note: A landfall for water, food, and news on both crossings from the earliest voyages, and after the permanent mission and garrison founded in 1668, a colonial dependency that the galleon supplied as its logistical lifeline. Earlier encounters with Chamorro communities involved barter and recurrent violence.

nodes.name: Taxco
nodes.note: One of the mining districts whose silver, refined and coined inland, fed the American side of the trade indirectly rather than through any direct shipment to the coast.

nodes.name: Zacatecas
nodes.note: A major silver-mining district supplying the coin that ultimately reached Acapulco for the westbound crossing, by way of Mexico City rather than any direct route to the Pacific.

nodes.name: Guanajuato
nodes.note: Another of the great mining districts whose output passed through Mexico City's mint before any of it could reach the Acapulco lading.

nodes.name: Mexico City mint
nodes.note: Coined the silver that mining districts across New Spain sent inland, producing the trusted specie that made up the bulk of the westbound cargo alongside the royal situado.

nodes.name: The permiso and boleta system
nodes.note: The legal cargo ceiling, fixed at 250,000 pesos outbound and 500,000 in return silver in 1593 and repeatedly raised thereafter, administered through cargo-space certificates called boletas that a prohibited but persistent secondary market moved into merchant hands. The Crown suppressed it by decree on 25 November 1813.

nodes.name: The situado
nodes.note: The royal subsidy remitted from New Spain because Philippine revenue never covered its own military and administrative costs, carried alongside merchant silver on the same westbound ships and financing everything from fortifications to the Marianas garrison.

nodes.name: Andrés de Urdaneta
nodes.note: An Augustinian friar with prior Pacific experience who planned and navigated the officially documented 1565 return, establishing the reproducible high-latitude route that institutionalized the tornaviaje. That his method became the credited one, over Arellano's earlier but less official arrival, was a matter of documentation and instruction rather than sole discovery.

nodes.name: Miguel López de Legazpi
nodes.note: Commanded the 1564-65 expedition, founded the Spanish base at Cebu, and in 1571 occupied and refounded Manila as colonial capital, converting an existing commercial node into the network's central hub.

nodes.name: Felipe de Salcedo
nodes.note: Legazpi's grandson, and captain of the San Pedro on the 1565 return voyage that reached Acapulco under Urdaneta's navigation.

nodes.name: Alonso de Arellano
nodes.note: Commander of the San Lucas, which separated from Legazpi's fleet and reached New Spain before Urdaneta's San Pedro, producing a priority dispute the later tradition resolved in Urdaneta's favor because his voyage was official, deliberately undertaken, and reproducible.

nodes.name: Antonio de Morga
nodes.note: An Audiencia official who recorded a documented eighty-one-day westbound crossing in 1595, converted the merchant ship San Antonio into the warship San Diego to fight Olivier van Noort in 1600, and later wrote Sucesos de las Islas Filipinas, the indispensable and self-interested official account of the system's first decades.

nodes.name: Domingo de Salazar
nodes.note: First bishop of Manila, whose 1590 report to Philip II on the city's Chinese physicians, artisans, and food sellers is the clearest direct evidence that the 'China trade' meant a complete urban supply relationship, not merely the arrival of silk.

nodes.name: Thomas Cavendish
nodes.note: Captured the Santa Ana off Baja California in 1587, the first major seizure to demonstrate both the eastbound cargo's value and the predictability of the galleon's final coastal approach.

nodes.name: Woodes Rogers
nodes.note: Captured Nuestra Señora de la Encarnación y Desengaño off Baja California in 1709, one of a small number of secure galleon captures that nonetheless shaped the lasting British image of a predictable Spanish treasure ship.

nodes.name: George Anson
nodes.note: Waited off Cape Espíritu Santo for the returning galleon and captured Nuestra Señora de Covadonga on 20 June 1743 after a fight, taking roughly 1.3 million pieces of eight and the ship's papers, which survive as an involuntary archive of the network. Manila financed its defenses against the memory of that loss for years afterward.

nodes.name: José Basco y Vargas
nodes.note: A reforming governor-general who pushed Philippine agricultural diversification and production, part of the broader late-eighteenth-century effort to reduce the colony's dependence on the single annual carrier.

nodes.name: Manila Consulado
nodes.note: The merchant guild chartered in 1769, converting a looser rhetorical community of 'the city and its commerce' into a defined corporation that regulated disputes, represented merchant interests, and administered the correspondencia underpinning the cargo-rights system.

nodes.name: Council of the Indies
nodes.note: The Madrid tribunal that legislated the trade's statutory framework in the Recopilación, adjudicated disputes referred from Manila and Mexico, and issued the repeated reissuances of cargo law that themselves suggest chronic noncompliance.

nodes.name: Royal Philippine Company
nodes.note: Chartered in 1785 to promote direct Spain-Philippines trade around the Cape of Good Hope, it coexisted and competed with the Acapulco service rather than replacing it outright, and outlived the galleon itself before an uneven career ended it in the 1830s.

nodes.name: The Chinese Sangley merchant community
nodes.note: Supplied most of Manila's commercial merchandise and much of its food and skilled craft labor, cultivating credit and compadrazgo relationships with Manila buyers even as the colonial government confined, taxed, expelled, and repeatedly attacked them, most severely in the 1603 massacre.

nodes.name: The Manila Galleon
nodes.note: The annual carrier itself, a Crown-chartered ship or pair of ships rather than a fixed fleet, that made every other part of the system physically possible. No single vessel or route defines it; it is tethered here to the ports and people it connected.

nodes.name: The correspondence chain
nodes.note: The information route by which Madrid's orders reached Manila and Manila's reports reached Madrid: Spain to Veracruz by fleet, Veracruz to Mexico City overland, Mexico City to Acapulco by courier, Acapulco to Manila by galleon. A single lost ship could postpone a decision by a year or more.

edges.note: The westbound crossing, faster and more direct: roughly seventy-five to one hundred twenty days, carrying coined silver, the situado, soldiers, friars, and news.

The eastbound tornaviaje, arced north through the Kuroshio extension and the North Pacific westerlies before turning south to the coast: commonly one hundred fifty to two hundred ten days, and considerably longer over the ground than the roughly 14,000-kilometer great-circle distance.
Fujianese merchants extended credit and cultivated compadrazgo and padrinazgo ties with Manila buyers to secure trade and protection, documented in a 1689 debt list and 1690 guild records.
